title: Longest Word in Dictionary through Deleting

content.title: Longest Word in Dictionary through Deleting

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given a string s and an array of strings dictionary, find the longest word in dictionary that can be formed by deleting some (possibly zero) characters of s while keeping the remaining characters in order. If multiple words tie for longest, return the lexicographically smallest one; if none can be formed, return an empty string.

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Formed by deleting some characters, keeping relative order\"","A classic subsequence check, done with two pointers in linear time per word"],["\"Longest, ties broken lexicographically smallest\"","Sorting the dictionary by (length descending, then lexicographic ascending) lets the FIRST valid subsequence found already be the answer"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

A word can be formed by deleting characters from s exactly when that word is a SUBSEQUENCE of s (its characters appear in s in the same relative order, not necessarily contiguously). Checking this for one word against s takes a simple two-pointer linear scan.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Longest Name Hidden Inside a Longer Phrase
blocks.text: Picture checking whether a short name's letters appear, in order, somewhere within a longer phrase (skipping over any other letters freely). Scanning the phrase once while trying to match the name's letters in sequence checks this directly.

blocks.caption: A word formable by deleting characters from s is exactly a subsequence of s

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: s = "abpcplea", dictionary = ["ale", "apple", "monkey", "plea"]
Result: "apple". "apple" and "ale" and "plea" are all subsequences of s, but "apple" is the longest.
Example: s = "abpcplea", dictionary = ["a", "b", "c"]
Result: "a". All three single-character words are subsequences (each of length 1), so the lexicographically smallest, "a", wins.
5. How Should We Think?

Before checking every single dictionary word against s and then comparing candidates for the tie-breaking rule at the end, notice that SORTING the dictionary first by the exact priority order needed (longest first, then lexicographically smallest) means the first word found to be a valid subsequence is IMMEDIATELY the final answer.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Checking whether a word is a subsequence of s is a standard two-pointer linear scan, independent for each word.

Observation 2: The answer must be chosen by two criteria in priority order, longest length first, then smallest lexicographic order among ties.

Observation 3: Sorting the dictionary array itself by exactly that priority (descending length, then ascending lexicographic order) means candidates are already visited in the exact order the final answer would be picked.

Observation 4: The first word in that sorted order which passes the subsequence check is guaranteed to be the correct final answer, since no later word could ever outrank it.
This leads to sorting the dictionary by (length descending, then lexicographic ascending), then returning the first word that passes the subsequence check.
6. Brute Force Solution
Check every dictionary word against s for the subsequence property, tracking the best answer found so far by directly comparing length and lexicographic order each time.
Why the code is written this way

items: Checking every word directly and tracking a running best answer implements the definition clearly.
This is already efficient for the given constraints; sorting first is a clean alternative that simplifies the tie-breaking logic into "return the first match".

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(number of words times (s length plus word length)) for all subsequence checks and comparisons.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the output.
Limitation: sorting the dictionary by the exact priority order needed simplifies "track the best so far" into "return the first valid match", avoiding repeated comparisons.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Sort the dictionary array by a custom comparator: longer words come first; among equal lengths, lexicographically smaller words come first. Then scan the sorted dictionary in order, returning the FIRST word that is a subsequence of s. Since the sort order already matches the exact priority used to pick the final answer, the first match found requires no further comparison against other candidates.
Sort the dictionary by (length descending, then lexicographic ascending); return the first word that passes the subsequence check.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run (sorted dictionary by length descending, then lex ascending: apple, monkey, plea, ale)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Word (in sorted order)","Subsequence of s?","Action"],"rows":[["apple","yes","FIRST match found, return immediately"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since the dictionary is sorted in EXACTLY the priority order the answer must satisfy (longest first, then lexicographically smallest among ties), the very first word encountered during the scan that passes the subsequence check is guaranteed to outrank every later word in the sorted order, making it the correct final answer without needing further comparisons.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(number of words times log(number of words)) to sort, plus O(number of words times (s length plus word length)) for subsequence checks.
Space: O(number of words) for the sort, O(1) extra otherwise.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Longest Word in Dictionary through Deleting combines a straightforward subsequence check with a clean sort-by-priority trick that eliminates manual tie-breaking comparisons.
Common Mistakes

items: Getting the sort comparator direction backward (ascending length instead of descending, or descending lexicographic order instead of ascending).
Forgetting that "deleting characters" means checking for a subsequence, not requiring the word to be a contiguous substring.

12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: subsequence check via two pointers, combined with sort-by-priority to simplify tie-breaking.
Core Idea: "formed by deleting characters, keeping order" is exactly the subsequence definition.
Time: O(n times (s length plus word length)) for both approaches, plus O(n log n) if sorting first.
Space: O(1) extra for direct comparison, O(n) if sorting.
Most Important Observation: sorting by the exact tie-breaking priority turns "track the best" into "return the first match".
Interview Difficulty: a clean, quick subsequence-check problem.
One line memory trick: subsequence check, sorted by longest-then-smallest first.
